title: Node.js Architecture & Express API Services
description: Node.js is an open-source, cross-platform JavaScript runtime environment built on V8. Express is a minimal web framework for building RESTful APIs.
detailedExplanation: Node.js operates on an event-driven, single-threaded I/O model backed by libuv threadpool for disk/network ops. Express uses a pipeline middleware pattern where incoming HTTP requests pass through functions sequentially before reaching final controllers.
architectureFlow: Client HTTP Request -> Express Middleware Stack (Cors, Helmet, Logger, Body Parser) -> Route Handler -> Controller -> Service -> Database -> Response
examples: Global error handler middleware with status code mapping
Streaming large files using Node.js streams to prevent memory leaks
Rate limiting middleware with Redis storage

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between process.nextTick() and setImmediate() in Node.js?
interviewQuestions.answer: process.nextTick() executes immediately after the current operation completes, before the event loop continues. setImmediate() executes on the next check phase of the event loop cycle.

interviewQuestions.question: Explain Express Middleware pattern and next() error propagation.
interviewQuestions.answer: Express middleware functions take (req, res, next). Calling next() passes control to the next middleware. Calling next(err) with an argument jumps directly to the 4-argument error handler middleware.

bestPractices: Always handle uncaught exceptions and unhandled promise rejections gracefully
Use helmet for security headers and rate limiting to prevent DDOS attacks
Use environment variables for secret credentials via dotenv or config vaults
commonMistakes: Blocking the main thread with heavy synchronous math operations (e.g. JSON.parse of 500MB string)
Forgetting return after res.json() inside conditional blocks leading to headers already sent error

title: Database Architecture: PostgreSQL, MySQL & MongoDB
description: Relational (PostgreSQL, MySQL) and Non-Relational (MongoDB) database management systems powering modern data persistence.
detailedExplanation: PostgreSQL and MySQL provide ACID compliant relational data structures with B-Tree indexes, foreign keys, and complex SQL joins. MongoDB provides document-oriented JSON/BSON storage ideal for horizontal sharding and flexible schemaless entities.
architectureFlow: Query -> Optimizer -> Index Lookup (B-Tree/Hash) -> Buffer Pool Cache -> Storage Disk / WAL Write
examples: PostgreSQL CTE (Common Table Expression) complex analytics query
Database migration scripts with atomic transaction rollbacks

interviewQuestions.question: What is ACID compliance in SQL databases?
interviewQuestions.answer: ACID stands for Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (valid state rules), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere), and Durability (committed data survives crashes).

interviewQuestions.question: How do B-Tree indexes improve database read performance?
interviewQuestions.answer: B-Tree indexes maintain sorted pointer structures that allow log(N) lookup time instead of O(N) full table scans, drastically speeding up WHERE and JOIN clauses.

sampleCode:
-- PostgreSQL Query with Window Functions
SELECT 
    department_id,
    employee_name,
    salary,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) as rank
FROM employees
WHERE status = 'active';
bestPractices: Index columns used frequently in WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY clauses
Use database connections pooling to avoid connection overhead per request
Use database migrations for all schema schema changes
commonMistakes: N+1 query problem caused by missing eager loads or joins in ORMs
Missing indexes on foreign key columns

title: Authentication, JWT Security & Redis Caching
description: Stateless and stateful authentication implementations using JSON Web Tokens (JWT), OAuth2, RBAC, and Redis for high-speed caching.
detailedExplanation: JWTs contain a base64 encoded header, payload, and cryptographic signature (HMAC-SHA256 or RS256). Redis operates as an in-memory key-value store achieving sub-millisecond read/write speeds, frequently used for session storage, caching, and rate limiting.
architectureFlow: Client Login -> Verify Password (Bcrypt) -> Issue Signed Access & Refresh JWT -> Client Stores Token -> Authorized Bearer Header Request
examples: JWT access + refresh token rotation workflow

interviewQuestions.question: How do Access Tokens and Refresh Tokens work together for secure auth?
interviewQuestions.answer: Short-lived Access Tokens (e.g. 15 mins) authenticate requests. Long-lived Refresh Tokens (e.g. 7 days) stored securely in HttpOnly cookies are used to obtain new access tokens without requiring the user to re-log in.

bestPractices: Never store sensitive passwords in plain text — hash with bcrypt or Argon2
Store Refresh Tokens in HttpOnly, SameSite, Secure cookies to prevent XSS attacks
Implement TTL (Time To Live) on all Redis cache keys to prevent memory leaks
commonMistakes: Storing JWT secret keys in source code repositories instead of environment variables
Storing sensitive PII (passwords, credit cards) inside JWT unencrypted payload
